column1: # hypothesis: A brush that provably cannot win the min/max chain inside a chunk can be deleted from the tape before the chunk is meshed
column2: and deleted BIT-EXACTLY. The bound is one sample per brush per chunk: a shape with declared Lipschitz constant l varies by at most l*r over a box of circumradius r
column3: so f(centre) +/- l*r encloses it. The exactness is a selection argument
column4: not an approximation one -- `apply(Add)` is IEEE min and `apply(Subtract)` is IEEE max
column5: both of which SELECT an operand rather than computing a new value
column7: so dropping a provably-losing Add or Subtract moves the result by zero ULP. The asymmetry is registered rather than discovered: smooth_min is exactly dominant at h == 0 and is NOT bit-exactly prunable in the losing direction
column8: because at h == 1 it returns b + (a - b)
column9: which is not bit-identical to a. Clause one: on a 64-brush stack of Add and Subtract spheres and capsules scattered over a 4x4x4 chunk world
column10: the median surviving-brush fraction per chunk is under 0.5. Clause two: meshing a chunk against the pruned tape is at least 1.25x meshing it against the full one. Clause three: every chunk's mesh is byte-identical between the two.

column1: # falsified by: A survivor fraction at or near 1.0
column2: meaning there is nothing to prune on a scattered stack and the mechanism has no purchase on this workload whatever the paper reports. Or -- the result that would matter far more -- any byte difference between pruned and full output on an Add/Subtract-only stack
column3: which would refute the IEEE selection lemma the whole mechanism rests on.
